newsitem.title: USA: United switches ad agencies after 31 years.
newsitem.headline: United switches ad agencies after 31 years.

text.p: For ad agency Leo Burnett, the skies over United Airlines turned unfriendly Friday.

The airline, a unit of Chicago-based UAL Corp., awarded its advertising business to New York-based Young & Rubicam and creative hot shop Fallon McElligott of Minneapolis, ending Burnett's 31-year hold on the account.

United's review of its $100 million advertising business -- one of the largest ad contests in airline history -- had agencies jockeying for months to oust the creator of United's familiar "Come fly our friendly skies" theme.

Burnett officials believed until the last minute that they still had a shot at keeping at least part of the business. Rumours circulated freely in the the bare-knuckled, much-hyped contest. Another agency, TBWA/Chiat Day, was widely reported to have won several days ago.
Some saw the breakup of United and Burnett, one of the marketing world's longest-running partnerships, as the end of an era.

Burnett, whose biggest account is Marlboro cigarettes, is the No. 1 U.S. agency with $2.48 billion in billings last year, Young & Rubicam is No. 10, with $2.14 billion and Fallon McElligott is No. 54, with $269 million in billings, according to Advertising Age.
The switch was a surprise since there were no signs United Airlines was struggling to overcome an image problem or slumping ticket sales. United is currently at the top of its game.

In the past two years since initiating its Employee Stock Ownership Plan, which placed 55 percent of the company in employee hands, United's stock price has more than doubled. Revenues last year hit $14.9 billion.
"I wouldn't see why they would need a change," said one Wall Street analyst who follows United. "The company is profitable. They're one of the biggest moneymakers in the U.S. airline industry."
"There is no loyalty anymore," said Jack Trout, managing partner of marketing strategy firm Trout & Partners based in Greenwich, Conn.

United's "Friendly skies" is one of those "grand old themes," says Trout. "The only thing left is to have Marlboro ride out of Burnett. (If) they fly away, it really says the historic relations that agencies have had with their clients -- their partnerships -- are over."

United has said the ad competition was part of a companywide "best practices" review, initiated at the time of the employee buy-out. But the announcement to re-examine the ad account came shortly after the retirement in late June of John Ruhaak, United's vice president-advertising and promotion for 22 years and a former Burnett veteran.

The review was conducted by David Coltman, senior vice president-marketing and Michael Howe, director-advertising and promotion, who assumed Ruhaak's duties. Howe had directed United's Mileage Plus frequent flier programme.

A changing of the guard in a company's marketing staff is one of the most common reasons for a company to consider a new advertising approach, says Ken Love, vice president-creative director at consulting firm Lippincott & Margulies.
"It's the easiest way to let people know that 'I'm in charge,'" says Love.
For agencies, it's a costly switch, since pitches alone can cost hundreds of thousands of dollars -- a high price for what some view as corporate chest-thumping.

But an even higher price may be paid by the corporation that switches agencies too often. Clients undertaking arbitrary reviews may end up chilling the creativity and candor they're seeking in an agency partner.
"It creates an enormous amount of fear in the business," said Trout. "It does not make for candor. It makes for 'Protect your billings at all costs.'"
